_comment: Every game ./gpb capture and ./gpb profile know about, and everything that differs between
them. Adding a game is adding a block here - no script changes.
This file is COMMITTED, unlike gpb.conf. Nothing in it is a secret or a property of one
machine: it is the shape of a game's network, which is the same for everybody working on
the project and is worth reviewing in a diff when it changes.
Paths are relative to this folder. Two games must never share ANY of the paths below -
once two games' addresses are mixed into one file there is no way to tell them apart again.
GpbGames.ps1 refuses to run while two games declare the same file, and every file is
declared per game rather than falling back to PUBG's name.
FIELDS
name              what the game is called, for messages and a new profile
watchProcess      process to wait for, WITHOUT .exe - Capture-GameTraffic -WatchProcess
probePort         UDP port the game probes datacentres on, to harvest landmarks;
null when the game has no such mechanism, and then no landmark is
collected and landmarkPath stays empty
observedPath      where capture appends the addresses it attributes to the game
landmarkPath      where capture appends probe endpoints; null when probePort is null
tcpSessionsPath   where capture -Protocol tcp writes its diagnosis
unverifiedPath    where the builder lists observed addresses it could not vouch for
manualCidrPath    ranges added by hand that the builder must keep
profilePath       the profile the builder writes; created on the first run if missing
awsRegions        AWS regions whose published EC2 ranges an observed address may belong to
azureRegions      the same for Azure
globalAccelerator true when the game is reached through AWS Global Accelerator. Those
anycast addresses are published only as GLOBAL /17s shared by every GA
customer, so a match is routed as exactly that /32 and never widened
asns              autonomous systems the game owns outright; their BGP-announced prefixes
(RIPEstat) count as published ranges, clamped like a cloud prefix
note              anything a person needs to know before trusting the numbers above
awsRegions, azureRegions, globalAccelerator and asns are the builder's cross-check: an
observed address inside none of them is treated as unverified and kept out of the profile.
A game with none of them declared gets no profile - see the note on cs2. That is not a
default to leave in place; it means the cross-check is missing, and ./gpb profile says so
rather than writing a profile that looks finished.
Whatever is declared, one game's profile never covers an address another game was observed
on: the builder narrows a block until it holds none of them, and Test-Profile.ps1 fails a
profile whose ranges overlap another game's.

pubg.name: PUBG
pubg.note: Gameplay is UDP on Azure and AWS Asia. The game picks its region by probing one endpoint per Azure region on UDP 8081, which is what probePort harvests. The lobby is TCP 40002 on an AWS Global Accelerator and is declared on the licence server, not here.

cs2.name: Counter-Strike 2
cs2.note: ./gpb profile does not build this game, and does not need to: the licence server keeps CS2's ranges equal to Valve's published relay list (web-service/scripts/sync-sdr.ts), and profiles/cs2-vn.json is the self-hosted copy of the same list. The rest of this note is why capture alone could not. CS2 carries gameplay over Steam Datagram Relay: the client talks UDP to a Valve relay PoP, not to the match server, so an observed address belongs to Valve's own network and matches no AWS or Azure range. The cross-check above is therefore empty on purpose and ./gpb profile will refuse rather than write an empty profile. What it needs instead is the PoP list Valve publishes for appid 730, which also removes the need to widen prefixes statistically the way PUBG does. Region ranking has the same problem: there is no UDP 8081 equivalent, so landmarks must come from that PoP list too - until they do, relays are compared on the first leg alone, which the client already handles and logs.

valorant.name: VALORANT
valorant.note: Riot publishes no server list: its peering page (riotgames.com/en/peering-information) gives BGP policy only. What IS public is what the cross-check uses. Vietnamese accounts play on the AP shard, Singapore and Hong Kong. Community captures (github.com/alexonpeace/valorant_servers, Feb 2026) put Singapore on Riot Direct 151.106.248.0/24 - announced by AS6507 - and on AWS Global Accelerator anycast addresses, which ip-ranges.json publishes only as GLOBAL /17s; hence asns and globalAccelerator. Tokyo (ap-northeast-1) is there for players the matchmaker spills over. Unknown until the first capture: whether the game probes regions on a port of its own (probePort stays null until one is seen, so nothing is ever mistaken for a landmark), and whether its latency probe shares the gameplay address the way CS2's does. Read the port column of the first capture before trusting the profile.

lol.name: League of Legends
lol.note:
Captured 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-22 from Hanoi, six sessions. Gameplay is UDP from League of Legends.exe, which only runs during a match - LeagueClient.exe is the lobby and is not watched (see lolc). Every session went to ONE server, 151.106.247.7 on UDP 7331, about 54 packets/s (120728 over 2233 s). Riot documents 5000-5500 and 7000-8000; 7331 is outside the first and the profile routes by address anyway, so never key anything on those ranges. 151.106.247.0/24 is announced by AS6507 exactly, so the profile routes that /24 and nothing wider. It does not overlap TFT (151.106.248.16/28) or VALORANT (151.106.248.0/28, 43.229.65.0/24); the builder's overlap rule decides that, never loosen it.

NO LANDMARK EXISTS, AND THAT IS WHY landmarkPath IS null. Measured 2026-09-23: the server answers no ICMP echo (20/20 lost), no TCP on 80, 443, 7331, 5223, 8080 or 2099 (no SYN-ACK and no RST), and none of the 1016 addresses in 151.106.246-249.x answer ICMP either. tracert dies after the ISP (Viettel, 27.68.236.211). So the client compares relays on the first leg only and cannot measure the player's own connection to the game - it cannot tell whether the tunnel helps. The candidate is the last hop before AS6507 that still answers, found by `traceroute -n -U -p 7331 151.106.247.7` from each relay and from a player's line; it is a landmark only if it sits within a millisecond or two of the server.

The game process's TCP is HTTPS 443 only - Cloudflare, AWS us-west-2, CloudFront - none of it Riot's AS and none blocked, so lobbyAddresses stays empty. Only one server has been seen, from one Hanoi line; players elsewhere may be put on another, and at 54/s discovery reports it.

lolc.name: League of Legends Client
lolc.note: The League of Legends lobby, captured for diagnosis only (TCP, 2026-09-22) - it is not a game to route. LeagueClient talks HTTPS 443 to Cloudflare (104.16-18.x, 172.64.x), AWS us-west-2 (35.8x.x), Google (34.111.148.117) and 32.18x.x.x, nothing in Riot's AS6507, nothing blocked. None of it is latency-sensitive, so never build a profile from this entry: everything in it would be routed through a relay for no gain. The match itself is League of Legends.exe - see lol.

tft.name: TFT
tft.note: Not captured yet. Riot publishes ports, not servers: the match is UDP 5000-5500 (and 7000-8000) from League of Legends.exe, which only runs during a match - LeagueClient.exe is the lobby and is not watched. Vietnam moved to Riot's own servers in January 2025 (VNG publishes), first hosted in Hong Kong, later on hardware in Vietnam. Whether those servers sit inside AS6507's announcements is unknown - an address outside them lands in observed-lol-unverified.txt, which is the first thing to read after a capture. AS6507 is also VALORANT's, so the two games may share prefixes; the builder's overlap rule decides that, never loosen it.

apex.name: Apex Legends
apex.note:
Captured 2026-09-20. Gameplay is UDP from r5apex_dx12.exe to Respawn's own EC2 space on ports 10000-10500, in ap-northeast-1 (Tokyo) and ap-east-1 (Hong Kong) - both seen carrying a match, so both are declared.

APEX MEASURES EVERY DATACENTRE, ON THE GAMEPLAY PORTS. Read this before judging any apex address. 216.244.0.0/16 is Respawn's block spread across 11 AWS regions - Tokyo, Hong Kong, Frankfurt, Ohio, Virginia, Oregon, Sydney and more - and the client measures them from the lobby on the same ports it plays on. So probePort stays null and landmarkPath stays null: there is no separate probe port to key on, Test-ProbeEndpoint can never classify one, and both the capture (-MinPackets 500) and the service (NewServerPackets 500 in a 30 s window) let those measurements through as if they were servers.

Tell them apart by RATE - not by geography, not by packet count, and NOT by seconds: a discovery row's window is bounded by the recorder's 30 s report and 60 s rest, so a real match reported by a client looks short next to one the operator captured end to end. A match runs ~140 packets/s from its first second; a measurement runs 25-60.
  216.244.36.123  123162 / 874 s = 141/s  ap-northeast-1  match     (capture)
  216.244.53.123   87948 / 627 s = 140/s  ap-northeast-1  match     (capture)
  216.244.26.243    8360 /  61 s = 137/s  ap-east-1       match     (discovery)
  216.244.14.228    2593 /  43 s =  60/s  eu-central-1    measured  (capture)
  216.244.19.192    1727 /  31 s =  56/s  eu-central-1    measured  (capture)
  15.129.62.15       690 /  28 s =  25/s  ap-east-1       measured  (discovery)
Under about 100/s is a measurement however long it ran and wherever it is. 15.129.62.15 was briefly routed as asia-hk 15.129.62.0/23 on 2026-09-20 on its region alone, before the rate was compared; dropped the same day with -AllowCoverageLoss. ap-east-1 is declared because of 216.244.26.243, not because measurements keep arriving from Hong Kong. Eight more - seven eu-central-1, one us-east-2 - were rejected on /admin/discovery that day. Never add a region to explain a measurement: routing a measured path is the landmark rule, the game would compare a tunnelled datacentre against direct ones and could pick the wrong one.

Apex ships two executables from the same install, r5apex.exe on DX11 and r5apex_dx12.exe on DX12, and only the one named above is watched; launching without the DX12 option means capture waits forever.

wot.name: World Of Tank
wot.note:
Captured 2026-09-21.

THE QUIETEST GAME MEASURED, AND THE REASON discoveryPacketsPerSecond EXISTS. A World of Tanks match runs 9-16 packets a second, against PUBG's 40-60 and Apex's 140, so the client's built-in threshold of 500 packets in 30 seconds - 16.7 a second - sits just above every server this game plays on. Measured through the tunnel on 2026-09-22: the busiest 30-second window of a whole match was 457 packets, 91 per cent of the threshold and never over it. Eight addresses in one capture, 12.9-14.9 a second, every one of them under.

There IS a burst - 543 packets in 6 seconds, about 90 a second - when a battle loads, and it would clear 500 on its own. It does not help. The recorder only listens once the tunnel has carried no match traffic for 15 seconds, so when the game hands you to a server the profile lacks, listening starts long after the burst is over; and a mid-session server change has no burst at all - 282 packets in 29 seconds when it moved on 2026-09-22 at 13:52:54. Discovery found a new server here only if the game started on one.

7 a second - 210 in a window - is under half the quietest match seen and four times the loudest address in any capture that was not a match. Raise it if this game's own idle traffic ever gets reported; do not raise it because a report was wrong for some other reason.

deltaforce.name: Delta Force
deltaforce.note: Not captured yet. The cross-check is empty on purpose until the first capture shows where the servers are, so ./gpb profile will refuse to build rather than write a profile that looks finished. Read the first capture before declaring anything: which provider and region the gameplay addresses belong to (then awsRegions, azureRegions or asns), the port column (whether the game probes regions on a port of its own - probePort stays null until one is seen), and the packets/second of each address, since a match and a lobby measurement are told apart by rate.
